name: Nox

backstory.title: Chapter I — World So Cold
paragraphs: The city was glinting dimly in the evening sun, the last rays of light cast upon the sky, painting Luyarnha in a deep red, the young city bustling with life, as people scouted the marketplaces in Paterna Iter and the train rolled into the station just to pour out more faces into the crowd. Dozens of merchants were presenting their wares to the visitors, offering vegetables and fresh meat, carefully crafted artworks and pieces, as well as the usual fabrics and raw material that could be found everywhere inside the walls.

The twins quickly dove behind a bunch of crates, hiding from the eyes of the cleric currently scanning the crowd in search of them. They had successfully sneaked away, leaving behind the Spired District and the cult of the Radiant Church in which they had grown up, constantly watched by its clergy. The two snickered as they rounded the next corner, finally leaving behind the man they kept evading for hours now. Making their way back home, the two continued their little bickering, laughing, as they chased each other after managing to nab two apples from a distracted merchant. It was fun while it lasted, as the two returned to the Church, seeing the silhouette of a tall woman waiting for them at the gate. Their mother stared down at her two sons, arms crossed, her expression betraying how truly screwed they were. In hindsight, they should not have run. Not only were they severely punished for their actions but both of them came down with an illness they must have caught on their adventure. At first it was not much but an ache in their bodies. Their daily tasks became harder and harder, until neither of them managed to carry the crates they were supposed to any longer. Solan had sat himself down on the floor, trying to stifle the rattling cough that both boys had to fight now. The initial unwillingness of the clerics watching over them to let them rest was quickly brought to an end, when a member of the Blood Cross took a look at them.

Nyctol sat on his bed, watching over his brother, who was writhing in his sleep. Normally it would be the other way around. His twin had always been stronger than him. And especially braver. He could talk for hours to people he did not know. He could carry whatever was needed, since he was ten years old. Everyone adored Solan. Except for their mother but in the end nothing could please her. They were never enough. Seeing his brother like this, defenceless, pale, the Pestilence visible on his hands and face, festering on the obsidian skin, his expression a mirror of his pain, it broke Nyctol more than the sickness ever could. Eunoia entered the room once again, taking a look at both of her children, as they laid sleeping, their bodies unable to enter the usual trance. It went to show how bad the two were doing in their recovery. She prayed to the Radiant One, kneeling in the centre of the room, unbeknownst to the twins. When she finished speaking the words into the warm air, she rose and walked over to the smaller boy. Looking down upon his lean frame that was shaking from the pain, she could not help but see their father in him. A man, who caused her too much pain, reflected in the child she wished to be able to love properly. Looking at his brother, the hand squeezing her heart, gripped it even harder. For the second time on this very day, she tried every spell but when she had arrived, the clerics had already warned her that something was not right, that their magic had not worked on either of the children, despite supposedly working on the other infected. And they had hoped that her magic would be stronger, that it would be enough but there was no sign of that. Thus she had to make a choice: Tend to both of her children, risking both their lives and lessening the chance of survival, or focus her attention on one of them, to at least save one of the two. When Nyctol managed to slowly open his eyes, he found himself in an empty room. White curtains were drawn closed, blocking out the sunlight and causing the room to be only dimly illuminated by its rays. Sitting up was everything but easy, his head spinning and the rest of his body unwilling to cooperate with him. Looking around, he saw only the empty bed, where Solan had rested a while ago. Dread crept up inside of him but he blocked it out. His twin was so much stronger and so much more resilient than him. If Nyctol had managed to recover, surely Solan would already be back to work and greet him with his big, kind smile that was only reserved for him. Surely.

So he forced himself to get up, seek out his brother and apologize for having suggested to go on their little adventure that had caused so much trouble. But when he pushed open the wooden door that felt way heavier than he remembered, all he saw was his mother talking to his father, who shed silent tears over a covered body lying on a surgery table to probably soon be picked up and disposed of. And when he heard his mother's voice saying three little words, which would haunt him forever, he could not help but weep. Because for some reason, that Nyctol could not hope to grasp, Solan was dead.

backstory.title: Chapter II — Leave It All Behind
paragraphs: When someone grasped his arm, Nyctol almost jumped away. Though he would not be able to escape his father's grapple if he tried to. The tall half elf was looking down at him, scrutinizing the younger. “What do you think you are doing?”

Nyctol finally managed to slip away from Candor, rubbing his wrist, that still held the letter he had written for someone very dear to him. He put himself between the thin sheet of paper and his father. But the blonde had other ideas, reaching for it, holding him in place. Still, the Shadar Kai avoided giving the letter up to his father successfully. “I'm just- Trying to deliver something!”, he gripped the paper tight, standing straight, trying to appear as tall as his father but failing. “To your little friend, right? Nyctol, listen.” Candor's stern gaze met his son's defiant eyes, “You cannot do that. I know you two have- something going on. But you are not a fighter. And you are definitely not getting out of fighting if you meet with someone like him! You know I'm not against-”

He motioned towards Nyctol, who, in turn, looked hurt by the implication. “No. But she is! And that is why you are here. Because she knew I would never listen to her words!” “If you do this, there is no going back! People will know! And if they don't know how to fix you, they will have to send you away! I don't want that to happen, son.” They looked at each other in silence. Candor had his hand outstretched, waiting for his son to hand over the letter. The younger was just staring at him, tears stinging in his eyes. Then, he finally gave it up. Fix him. All he was, was someone to be fixed. According to the one person who held no judgement, no ill will towards him. He wondered if his father was right. If he was broken. Not only physically, not only because of his scarred lungs, because of his weakness or frail constitution but simply because of who he was. Of who he dared love. Was it so wrong?

In the middle of the night, Nyctol had climbed to the roof of the church, able to look out into one part of the Spired District. And he wondered what was holding him back, what was keeping him here in this place. It would be so easy to just let it go, take the leap, maybe have more luck next time. Why did he stay? Why was he doing this to himself? His brothers ridiculed him, his mother hated him and the only one of whom he thought cared about him, believed him to be broken. To be something that had to be fixed. He did not realise he was crying, until a few droplets softly hit his skin. And then he figured why not end it, before it could get any worse. Not that he thought it could. He slowly drew to his feet, standing at the edge of the roof. He could see the Cathedral from here, the Castle, the main street of Paterna Iter. None of it was going to miss him, not a single part of this town. But then, just as he hovered his foot above the empty air, ready to step forward, he hesitated. Why should he leave this world behind without leaving any sign of himself. How was that fair? Was that supposed to be the end he deserved as just another nobody?

There was so much more to see, so much more to feel in this city and in this world. And here he stood, ready to throw all of it away, waste his chance. Any chance. At showing all of them what he was capable of. What he was truly worth. He owed it to himself. And he owed it to Solan. Not in this quiet night, he swore. While the moon was watching over him, he made a promise. He would grow as a person. He would grow into someone strong enough to pave his own way. To one day return and show them all that he was not broken and he would never break. But to do such thing, he realised, he could not stay. Strapped down by their ideals and their rules, he could not live. There was no use of being alive if he could not be himself, if he could not be free. He had packed only a few necessities, looking down at the letter, he had in the end picked it up and taken it with him, dropping the emblem of the Radiant Church onto the table in its stead. The mark on his skin remained but it hardly mattered now. Standing outside the building, he looked back one last time, making a promise that he would not come back. Not unless he was a different man. And so he left it behind, just like the Spired District. If there was one place no one would ever think to search for him, it would be the Shrouded District. And so he made his way there. Not looking back a second time.

backstory.title: Chapter III — Of Freedom and Fears
paragraphs: When Nox pulled the trigger, his heart felt like it was torn apart just like the throat of the man he just killed. He had not taken a life before. Not like this at least. Not with the intent to kill. Not without giving the other a single chance. But here he was, shrouded in darkness, listening to the panicked screams of the people around him, as the bloodied corpse hit the floor not far from him. His target had been an ill tempered merchant, who had his hands in businesses that did not concern him. And the bounty was high enough for him and his friends to pay for a small building to live in. But there was no way around getting his hands dirty for them. It did not matter that he had to do this. It did not matter that someone had to die. This was his world now. And despite the pain it caused, it also caused him to feel one thing for the first time: freedom.

He took to the roofs, able to overlook the dimly lit street, which had been thrown into complete disarray by Nox himself. He felt so close to the sky, it was almost suffocating, almost caging him in anew. It was weird to think of the open sky as a cage, as something that was keeping him in, weighing him down. But then again he wondered if there even was anything like freedom. Was it more than just a utopian concept for the poor unfortunate souls tied down by people who did not understand them? Or who did not agree with who they were? It was a thing people wanted to believe in, needed to believe in. He was not any different. He desperately held onto the hope of freedom.

The assassin almost tripped over the edge of the roof, catching himself just in time. Staring down into the dark below him, he halted. An image appeared, of his own bullet burying into the thin flesh of his neck, striking through veins and arteries, blood staining the floor beneath him, even before his airways were torn into shreds by the metal. He tried to cover the wound, tried to keep himself alive, tried to grasp at the life, which was slowly slipping away from him. His panicked eyes met the ones of his murderer, his own eyes staring back at him, as the light faded from them and they lost their focus. Dropping to his knees, arms wrapped around himself, Nox felt hot, unwanted tears running down his face, hitting the dusty stone beneath him. Drip. Drip. Drip.

And then those tears stopped. Replaced by thin droplets of blood, caught on his hands, staining them red. His breathing hitched, as he withdrew, hands shaking, pulling at his hair to come back to himself. From the darkness reached a hand, stretching towards him, asking, begging, to be taken. To be followed into the inky void. And he recognised the call, he recognised the voice, seeking its brother. And then he hit his back on the wall behind him, calling him back to reality, waking him from the dark dream. He was still crying, his breath came in short heaves as the panic squeezed his chest. He never wanted it. He was so sorry. He should not have convinced his brother to come with him. He should not have pulled the trigger on the merchant. He did not have the right to take someone's life. How even dare he? Finally he pulled himself up, walking back to the edge of the roof, looking into the dark, wondering if they would welcome him, swallow him, extinguish his fire like a snuffed out candle. It is not your time yet. He did not turn. He did not question where that thought came from. That voice, which held so much familiarity and was still so foreign. The voice that had told him to run. The same voice that had called for him so many times. He knew it was strange. He knew it was wrong. And still, it felt like a sought-for embrace, like a safe haven. So different from the cold world haunting his every move. And despite everything in him telling him that he should not listen to that voice. That it was not on his side, he did listen and he stepped back from the edge.

Nox pushed open the door without another word. The dark wood scraping across the floor, announcing the assassin to the people in the room. Kadar was sitting at the table on the other side of the room. Jith's eyes were also locked upon the Shadar Kai, who now turned to the person he had just killed for. The man smiled brightly at seeing the bloodied bullet. “I trust everything has been well taken care off then?” In turn, he only got a short nod of confirmation, which broadened his grin further, as he dropped a pouch of gold onto the table in front of Kadar. Jith quickly picked up the pay, looking into it to judge if it was the correct amount. When the youngest criminal seemed pleased, Nox nodded. Kadar in turn, stood up, walking over to his friend, “Are you alright? Did anything happen?” “Everything is fine.”

backstory.title: Chapter IV — What Hides in the Dark
paragraphs: When the gate behind him fell shut with a loud metallic bang, Nox spun around, flintlock readied to shoot, until it was knocked up by the guard's sword. The bullet hit nothing but the stone wall above him. Drawing back, both to get out of the weapon's reach and get room to think, sent him right into the arms of another guard of the crown. How had they even seen him coming? No time to think, as the warhammer of the second man was advancing towards him. With no other choice, he dropped himself onto the floor, scurrying away. Only that the defender had no intention of letting that happened, as the hammer crushed against Nox' leg. The horrific sound of splintering bone was all but drowned out by the scream that the assassin did not manage to bite down. When the sword fighter walked up to the downed man, he did not expect to come eye to eye with a reloaded flintlock, barely dodging a bullet to the eye. Nox vanished into thin air, before reappearing on a ledge above, unbeknownst to both enemies and readying another shot. Once he took down these two, there would surely be a whole squadron waiting for him just outside the gate. He would have to find the others and get out of this castle, before-

The arrow striking into his shoulder caught him off guard. Never had he thought he would so easily become the target of a surprise assail, especially several times in such a short while. He hissed, as he grasped for the arrow and twisted its wooden shaft until it broke, leaving only the metallic tip to lessen the bleeding. Then, when he locked eyes with the archer, he was the first to move, sniping down the ropes, which were securing some barrels that now came tumbling down towards the archer. This revealed his position to his other enemies though.

Thinking fast, Nox scanned the wall behind him, spotting a small, barred-off vent. On the other side was what appeared to be a hallway inside the castle. Not seeing an enemy in it, he vanished again and found himself on the other side momentarily. Taking a deep, rattling breath, trying to catch himself, he heard steps coming from both in front of him and behind him. Leaning heavily against the wall, his leg entirely useless, he took aim at the hallway, waiting for a guard to appear. But instead, skidding to a halt, rounding the corner across from Nox, was Kadar. Reacting quickly, the blonde sprinted over to him, shocked at the sight of the mangled leg, “Are you alright?” Kadar himself was sporting a few bruises and cuts but seemed okay, much to Nox' relief. Nox, in turn, laughed humourlessly, accepting the help of his most trusted ally. Maybe they would get out of this after all, seeing as they found each other. Maybe- When a blunt weapon struck the back of his head, Nox had no chance to react and neither did Kadar, as the informant was grappled and restrained by yet another guard. Despite having heard the five men growing closer, the two criminals had simply not caught up fast enough to escape from them.

The first thing he noticed, when Nox woke up was Kadar hovering over him. The second thing was that there were only four people around him. “Thank the gods, I thought we lost you”, the mastermind rogue mumbled, making the other furrow his brows. “A knock on the back of the head won't take me out, don't worry.” “What? Nox, you were run through by a fucking sword, I literally had you bleeding out in front of me!” His hand snapped towards his core instinctively, eyes falling upon the bloody cloth wrapped around his torso. “But you were- You were there when they struck me down, how- What happened then?” Kadar looked as confused as Nox felt. “I was not. Whatever happened, I was nowhere near you.” After several moments of silence, the white haired assassin spoke up, “Where is Jith?” At first he thought no one would answer him, as he sat propped up against the wall, barely feeling his limbs from the loss of blood. Then Cam spoke up, “He- is the one who ratted us out-” His next words were cut short, as the metal door swung open, revealing none other than Reinholdt Silverblood, two guards stationed behind him. Nox raised the small blade he had hidden, teleporting before him, ready to take down the king. Leave something behind. But instead, he was struck by the back of a lance right into his fresh injury. “Your little friend was right about keeping our guard up around you.” Reinholdt looked down upon the dark elf writhing on the ground.
“Now. It would be too sad to have your little gang go to waste. With all your talents... I have an offer-”

backstory.title: Chapter V — A Nameless Horror
paragraphs: In a dimly lit room, somewhere behind the ancient library, a lone silhouette stood leaning over an ancient eldritch tome, its secrets too dark, too dangerous for anyone outside its Order to delve into. Lending its power to its disciples, the being that had created the tome watched, as its newest student mastered its teachings quicker than the old masters. Curiosity mixed with pride, as it allowed the dark elf to continue scouring the pages for untouched knowledge.

Nox furrowed his eyebrows, as the pages before him sprung to life and revealed more to him than before. Unsure if any other member of the Order knew about this, he read on about the being which was described in the tome. It was frightening as much as it was fascinating, he realised, as he read further and further into the nameless horror, that he unwittingly served by following the royal family's orders. Swallowing the light, engulfing the world in tenebrous darkness, with each living being knowing exactly the same as everyone else. No secrecy, no plans that might lay in shadow, for everyone to be able to act of their own accord, to act in their best interest while having all the knowledge in the world. It wanted to create its own. Become a god that would allow everyone and everything under its influence to be entirely their own, to be free. And it wished in return for the world's light. To feast on its power. To throw the world into inky blackness.

The Shadow Rogue wanted to back off. Wanted to tell his brothers and sisters in the Order and hear their thoughts on this, but he could not draw away from the words, that echoed in his mind, filled every fibre of his being. This being granted them the power to kill, only to gain more influence, to fulfil its bidding and play right into its nefarious hands. Dread grasped at Nox' heart, squeezing, strangling his every thought. It did not wish for mere believers, for priests or for acknowledgement of the living. It wished for followers, for killers that would act for it, to bring darkness. It wanted to swallow the sun and replace it with itself. It would give everyone the same chances, the same knowledge, it did not want to control them or have them be the same, it strived for equality, not uniformity.

It strived against the Church's teachings, against their natural craving for light. It offered a new sort of hope. But was it a better one, Nox wondered. Was this worth it? Would this be a better way of living? A fairer one? As he reached the end of the page, he hesitated. This insatiable need to know let go of his mind, it was offering him to step away and continue living the same way he did before. His hand graced the edge of the page. He could read on. Could learn more about this eldritch being, that sought for his interest, his loyalty.

After another moment, Nox closed his eyes, shutting the tome and stepping back. Looking around, he saw nothing but the inky blackness, which was twisting and turning around each and every corner, seeping into the cracks and the empty space between the bookshelves. There was nothing in it, no movement, no inconsistencies, but this feeling of being watched did not leave Nox, as he walked out of the room, passing through an illusory shelf. As the hours passed, Nox could still feel the eyes of the Shadows on him, his neck prickling, his mind shouting at him that he should turn around and look for whatever was watching his every move. But he knew what it was. He could feel it listening, when he spoke to Kadar about what he had learnt. He could feel it following him, as he moved out to follow the royal's orders. He could feel its smile, as the life seeped out of his victim. He could feel its joy, as it watched him vanish back into the Shadows.

As he sat on his bed, consisting of a thin mat on the ground, seeking to finally enter his trance and lay off this feeling of exhaustion that was weighing down his bones and clouding his thoughts, he could hear its whispers. So close to his ear, that he thought it might grasp at him any moment now. Do you not want to know? It asked over and over again. Do you not seek the answers to all your questions? Nox forcefully shut his eyes, trying to block out the voice. Why did he leave? Why did she never love you and your brother? Why do they hate you so much? Only a few moments later a dark silhouette once again scourged through the library and into the room behind it. The ancient tome opened – the layer of dust on top of it, way too much, as only a few hours had passed, gently slid off its surface – a dark eye glinting in the dark, gleefully aware of the change in its follower's stance.

backstory.title: Chapter VI — Checkmate
paragraphs: Nox had made it into the room without problem. Engulfed in shadows, he watched his target, as she dusted of the chessboard and each of its pieces one by one, a serene smile on her face. She knew not of the worries of the common folk. Nor did she care. The nobles never cared. It was only ever about their politics and their money, never about the misfortune they caused for every other person around them. He manifested his umbral rifle, its shadows wrapping around his arm and melting into the flesh, inseparable from him unless he put it down himself and he aimed it at the unsuspecting woman. “I knew they would send one of yours after me. But I must admit it is quite an honour to have it be you”, she did not turn around, as she spoke. Only when the white king was dusted off and put back down, did she glance at the shadow he was stationed in.

“The Silverbloods never agreed with my actions.” She put down the piece of cloth, gaze swerving towards the window. “It was but a matter of time.” The assassin knew he should pull the trigger. Put her life to an end. But this woman was so uncannily calm, so at peace with death and something in Nox wanted to know how, wanted to know why. He was still silently aiming at her, the noble's gaze not quite finding him, betraying the fact that despite her ancestral ability to see in darkness, she could not quite see him. “Might I at least see the person, who shall take my life now?” Nox furrowed his eyebrows, “Why?” “I was never fond of the dark, it swallowing all colour. I don't want to die to it.” “No” Her gaze fell, still, he could see the tears glinting in her eyes. “I meant why do the Silverbloods want you dead? I looked into you. You are not of big influence, you hold barely any political power. In my eyes, you are no threat.”

She frowned, maybe taken aback, maybe hurt by his words. He did not bother clarifying. Instead of answering, the redhead walked towards the window, gaze locking on the dim stars in the sky and then onto the city beneath it. “To the Silverbloods I am. You know, most of my money is spent on this city. The orphanages, the doctors-” “So you give your money away. And-?”, now that she mentioned it, he noticed the undecorated room. No ornaments, no weird figures that most nobles seemed to love, no indulgence. Except for that one chessboard in the centre of the room. “It takes away from the things they do 'to help'. Every copper that is given by most royals is due to them wanting to appear more generous. For the public eye to look upon them with admiration and deep devotion.” “How are you different then?” She smiled. “I don't know if I am. I doubt it. Everyone acts for their own benefit. There is no such thing as selflessness, generosity... I want to make this city better. That is all. And whether my money helps or not, I will at least have tried my very best. For my own good or for the people's.” Silence fell. Nox contemplated the thought. Kindness, generosity, selflessness, love. Did any of it fit into a world like this? Did it exist at all? He stepped into the dim light, leaving the shadows, that had clung to him like ivy to the walls of Carmella's Greenhouse. She seemed calmer at actually seeing him, having turned towards him again. His gaze fell on the chessboard once more. When she noticed, she seemed almost apologetic. “I could not bear to sell it. It was a gift of my father's.” She caressed one of the white pawns, “You know how to play?” He walked over, rifle low at his side. “No.”

She sat down at one side of the table. “Then how about we play one game? You know, as a kind of- goodbye to this world?” Nox hesitated, his instincts told him to not agree to it, to dispose of her and get away. He had never failed a mission. But in the end, how would a game of chess avert the inevitable? He would kill her in the end. Slowly dropping into the other seat, Nox looked at the black set of figures in front of him. “Alright. White begins. Do you know how the pieces can move?” The assassin shook his head and Vassia proceeded to explain. Never before had he used the name of one of his targets, too worried he might loose his focus. And his will to kill. But there was a first time for everything, was there not.

backstory.title: Chapter VII — A Dark Blessing
paragraphs: The Shadow Rogue slowly walked down the corridor of the Silverblood Castle. He wondered if he would have felt more at home if this were the old building where the Radiant Church resided in, or if he would feel exactly as estranged and wrong within its walls. He would expect it to be the latter of the two. He could feel the walls watching him, ancient eyes lurking in the shadows to seep in any and all knowledge it can gather. It watched, as its disciple went to report his latest success. After all a successful return to the castle was the usual with the Order of Shadows. Nox bowed to the king, confirming the death of one Vassia Stedfort. Reinholdt Silverblood rose to his feet. “What marvellous words for my ears to feast upon. Today shall be a grand one, as a threat to my wonderful city has been diminished.”

The assassin knew better than to break his bow or dare speak up. Only when he heard the king address him, telling him he was dismissed for today, did he slowly get up to walk away. When he rounded the corner, he stopped short of running into Kadar, who also halted just in time to avoid a collision. “Ah, 13, I assume you return as bearer of good news?”, he patted the other's shoulder, who in turn nodded faintly, when he stopped the movement, his tone dropped lower, barely audible even with the other's sharp senses, “Listen. About that- thing you told me about. Maybe we should not delve further into its teachings. Maybe it might actually pose a threat.”

There was a moment of silence between the two, before Nox shook his head. “We are thirteen assassins overall, currently only eleven, I do not believe we could grant it enough power to actually swallow the light. Ever. Also I fear turning away from this now would not change a single thing, except result in our deaths.” Kadar did not answer, thus prompting his brother in the Order to walk away. The rifle at the dark elf's side side grew colder with each and every step, the shadows that were seeping under his skin, twisting into his arm, started grasping harder, cutting into him like blades. His arm felt as if it were burning with cold fire, causing him to drop his rifle, as he clutched the agonizing limb. Something moved in the shadows behind him, soundless, as it grew ever closer, its empty eyes stalking its target like a predator its prey. After a silent moment, in which Nox bit down any pained noise that threatened to spill, it shot out towards him, claws outstretched and when it finally reached the assassin, instead of exploiting his timely weakness, it landed on his shoulder. The pain vanished, when something lightly touched Nox' shaking frame. He looked in wonder at the shadowy creature that had landed and had managed to soothe his agony instantly. Its bone-white eyes watched him carefully, warmly, filled with curiosity, the night-black feathers ruffled up, had shadows seeping out of their tips and gently connecting to the shadowy streaks around his own frame. “What are you?”, he muttered into the air between the owl-like being and himself. In turn it inclined its head to the side, cooing faintly. And then he heard its voice in his head. “I was sent by your god, as a gift.” “A gift? For what? What god? The Shadow?”

“That is what you call them, yes”, the owl flapped its wings. “And who are you?”, he questioned, as the bird hopped off his arm flew in front of him. “My name is not comprehensible for mortal ears. I am a far spawn of the Giver.” “Is that its name? The Shadow's I mean?” “It is what I call him”, the bird landed, “If I were to name myself in a way for you to say, it would be Malik. The Giver's name is no different. But it is not my concern what mortal name you use for them or me.” “I see. It is nice to meet you, Malik. Though I have to ask: Why are you here? What did I do that the Giver decided to- 'reward' me?” “You wished to know more about them. They wish to learn more about you. That is what they desire. And they want to help you acquire whatever it is you desire.” Nox fell silent at this, gaze flickering towards the shadows. So be it. The only one, who questioned the sudden appearance of the shadowy owl was Kadar, though he was quickly dismissed by his friend, who told him that he had gained the service of a familiar, when he had been out training. Malik and Nox quickly grew into an effective team, both being silent, stealthy and perceptive. With every passing day they became more deadly, a duo from which you could never escape, only noticeable by a slight movement in the shadows, before the assassin would descent onto his target, like an owl would on a mouse.

backstory.title: Chapter VIII — Post Mortem
paragraphs: “Checkmate.” Nox sighed, watching his King fall. “I'll never beat you, will I?”, the assassin smiled faintly, taking the piece from his friend and twisting it between his fingers in contemplation. “You almost did. Twice, actually. But then you decided to try and promote your pawn, instead of attacking.” “A pawn cannot beat a king.” The woman shook her head faintly. “Not without a mistake on the enemy's side. But it can beat other pieces easily enough”, she concluded, picking up her fallen pieces from the side of the board. Nox fell silent at this, watching her in contemplation. “I suppose it would be similar to your job. People do not expect you and that eases the kill, does it not?”, she looked up from the queen, that she had just placed back on the board. Nox hummed in response, causing her to slightly squint at him, “Is that, why you did not kill me? Because I noticed you?”

“No.” He did not move from his position, arms crossed defensively, continuing to think in stoic stance. “Then why? You know my story, you know my name. And me? I know nothing about you. Not even your name. We have known each other for over a year now. And I have no idea why I am still alive. Why you let me live. Do you even know how that feels?”, her tone grew desperate. “I do.” Silence fell once again. Only the faint sound of the earth shifting around them and the railway in the distance loudly rattling away could be heard in the dimly lit room. “Because you are kind. And brave. And you actually care a great deal about this city and its people.” Nox spoke in a faint but sincere tone. “And when you told me about your family and about your feud with the Silverbloods and why they hated you... I couldn't take your life.” “I never expected someone like you to be so...” “Weak-willed? Cowardly?”, Nox suggested. But Vassia, in turn, seemed to disagree. “Kind.” She corrected. He green eyes showed no sign of deceit. As always, she was truly honest. The assassin seemed unconvinced still, “I don't know if that is a good thing for someone like me.” “Quite a double-standard, is it not?”, she questioned, though she asked for no answer, “You let me live, because of said kindness but with you it is a problem?” “I am not like you.” He uncrossed his arms, picking the king back up and placing the black piece on the board, before pointing at the white queen, “This is your role in this. The white queen. The good one. Luyarnha is made better by your kindness. And you are its strongest piece.”

He then picked up a black pawn. “This one is me. I'm a nobody. I'm only useful for one thing. Killing or being killed. I'm nothing but a weapon for them. And a weapon can have no feelings.” “That is not the truth. If you had no feelings I would not be alive, correct? And if we are already building upon this chess-allegory, you know full well how important the pawns are in the endgame. And how they can be promoted to any other piece on the board.” She poked his chest over the table. “That makes you just as important, if not more important than me.” He shook his head, smiling at her words, despite not fully believing them. “You truly are something aren't you?” She simply smiled at that and pointed at the board. As the new game started, Nox could not help but wonder how important a single pawn truly might be. Every black and white piece that fell to the other side felt as if it were representing the people of Luyarnha, the political warfare, the persons that had to fall, just so that the Silverbloods could keep their power. He looked at his black king, deciding that Reinholdt Silverblood was not the one he would fight for. He fought for the people of Luyarnha, to one day have them be free of unfair rulers and manipulative cults. Only the kings, a white bishop and a black pawn were left on the board. And after beating the bishop, which Vassia had used to check Nox' king, with the black pawn, said pawn reached the other side of the board and was quickly promoted to set the enemy king checkmate.

Vassia smiled at this development, “See? I told you a pawn can win you the game.” “Admit it, you let me win”, he muttered, as he held the white king between two fingers, wondering what this might represent. The noblewoman shook her head no, still smiling, “I did not. I could not have played that better. And neither could you.” “Well, thank you.” As he put the king back down, she held up the black pawn. “Hero of the hour”, she smiled, before putting down the small figure as well, gaze resting on the board. Nox laughed silently. A few minutes passed in silence, before he spoke up. “Vassia? The name's Nox.”

backstory.title: Chapter IX — Sacrifice
paragraphs: Slipping through the cracked wall and into the building, Nox left behind the darkened streets the Church did not care for. The room, which he found himself in seemed empty, not only void of colour as it was filled with inky darkness, but also of life. Or so it seemed for a long moment, until, finally, something moved at the other end of it. A door was pushed open and an elven man entered, closing the door swiftly behind him. Nox did not need to check twice to recognize him. Zenathin Fireil took a good hard look at the papers on his desk, trying to decipher the ancient script. His eyes scoured the shadows around him, locking onto Nox, who in turn, was frozen in his stance. “I never thought the first time coming face to face with you, would have your rifle between us.” The older Shadar-Kai sighed, scooping the papers into a pile and resting his arms on the now cleared table. “Please come forward, I would prefer to see my son's face, when he takes my life.” The assassin did not move an inch, causing his target to draw back to his full height. “I know you wish to take my life. Though I wish for you to know, you would be playing into their hands, do exactly what they expect you to. And doom yourself to be their little pawn.” As Nox drew forward, slowly, he could feel the shadows that were clinging to him slowly withdrawing, letting go of him and revealing him to Zenathin. The two had an uncanny resemblance, Nox being the living, younger image of his father. “What do you mean by that?” “The Church is looking for a way to get rid of me. If you take my life, all they have to do is kill you and tell everyone you were the one who took me down. Because having one of their own Templars doubt them would ruin their reputation.”

“Doubt? Why would someone like you doubt the Radiant Church?”, Nox still had his rifle trained on his father's head. This prompted no reaction from the elder, though. “Why do you think? It was them, who kept me from the person I fell in love with. It was them, who kept me away from my children. Nyctol, there was nothing I would not have given to watch you and your brother grow up. To watch you live your life and become-” “Solan is dead. He died when we were thirteen. You never would have had the chance anyway- And if you cared, you would have known this, so don't claim to love, when you have never felt that feeling before.”   “He is- What? When? How did he-”, Zenathin's eyes betrayed his feelings, shock, grief, regret. Nox would have felt pity for him, if it were not for the anger engulfing his every thought. The silence between them hung heavy, as Nox watched his father comprehend these news, that had apparently not reached him, even after 62 years. “How do you know so much about me, recognised me in the shadows, while not knowing of my brother's death?” The assassin did not hide his mistrust, the weapon between them practically serving as a shield. “Because the Church has their eyes on you, they watched you for years. I never thought not hearing of Solan could mean- I'm so sorry. If I had been there-” “What? Maybe you could have saved him?! He would not have had to die?! What would have changed?!”, the assassin took a step closer, Zenathin did not move, even as the weapon was pushed against his chest. “I could have been there for Solan, before he- And I could have been there for you.” Nox had not noticed he was crying, until a tear fell from his chin. Zenathin was watching him silently, not saying anything. “Fuck”, the younger cursed, lowering the weapon and turning to look away. His father still did not raise his voice, nor did he move. He could not believe he was doing this. Putting down his weapon, once again, letting his target live again. He heard the voice in the back of his mind, questioning what he was doing, questioning why he was too weak to do what he was tasked with once more. The first time had been bad enough, it scolded, before falling silent. Steps falling behind the door across from him drew Nox' attention away from his father, who now appeared to notice it too.

The assassin drew back, ready to vanish back into the shadows, when the door was thrown open, kicked in by on of the Templars. Light flooded the room now, pooling into it like a wave and washing away Nox' hope of getting away quietly. The two Grey Templars had their weapons drawn, openly readying themselves to attack, not taken aback by the assassin in the slightest. Instead the one in the front pointed his longsword at the older Shadar-Kai. “Zenathin Fireil, you are charged with treason and conspiring with the enemy on behalf of the Radiant One himself. Resisting will only make it worse for you”, he turned the weapon on Nox, “And your son.” They knew about him, about his family, about his alliances. What else did they know? He readied his shot. From his position he could spot Zenathin's hand sliding to the hilt of the longsword at his side. “I would understand correctly there is no way around spilling blood in this instance, is there? Still I implore you to put down your weapons, so we can settle this peacefully.” The blonde man shook his head slowly, “As you stated yourself: There is no way around spilling blood.” With that, he lunged, the two longswords clashing into each other. The elf was faster than his enemy though, using his momentum to get a bit of distance between them and driving the sword upwards. When the weapon struck true, a second passed where nothing happened but then radiant chains wrapped themselves around the enemy Templar, locking him in place.

Nox, not far behind, seized the moment to unleash his shot. There was no noise, no indication of the weapon firing in the first place, except for the telltale noise of rapid metal meeting bone and a pained expression on the sword fighter's face. Though he could not move freely, he could still reach far enough to try and land a blow on the man in front of him. But the older Rogue merely sidestepped the attacks without any problem. Focus still lying on the fighter, neither of them saw the other's attack coming. When the arrow struck Now square into the shoulder, his scream was momentarily drowned out by the booming thunder emanating from the shot, practically detonating in his face, throwing him into the wall behind him and off his feet. The world was spinning. Everything around Nox was blurry, little sparks of light dancing in his vision, blinding him to his surroundings. Nothing was clear, except for the searing pain pulsing through his every fibre. Then someone pulled him up, causing another wave of pain. As his vision slowly cleared, Zenathin turned back around, bracing himself for the next round of attacks that would surely follow, all the while shielding his son from the archer's view.

The older elf successfully dodged the first blow, parrying the second not quite as well, the enemy managing to graze his side. Both sniper and archer took their shots. Both bullet and arrow struck true. The archer's eyes widened, as his last seconds ticked away, the small hole in his forehead pouring blood momentarily, while the hind half of his scalp and brain now slowly dripped down the wall, gathering into a puddle on the ground. Zenathin on the other hand, was gasping in pain, as sharp tendrils made from blood wrapped around his arms and torso, digging through his armour and into the obsidian skin below. He tore some of them out of his arm, before lunging at the remaining foe.

The swordsmen traded blows. Then the enemy's eyes fell on his fallen comrade for but a moment, before locking on Nox. The assassin tried slipping away from him, but the blonde was not having it, cutting off his path and raising his sword to strike down the shorter elf. He flinched. He had come face to face with death but here there was no escaping it this time. No place to hide, no way to run, he could not even see behind his enemy, if he tried. He closed his eyes in sheer despair. But no pain followed. Only a shattering clash of metal. Nox opened his eyes in the exact moment, Zenathin struck his weapon into his enemy's abdomen. The assassin's reflexes kicked in within but a second, raising his rifle to the fighter's face and pulling the trigger. And with that the fight was over. Nox fell back against the wall, allowing himself the smallest smile. He was about to speak up, when his smile died on his lips.

Zenathin slowly sunk to his knees, clutching his torso, where he had – unbeknownst to Nox until this very moment – been run through by the blade of his enemy. The last remaining tendrils on his arms again tightened, causing the already shivering man to silently gasp in pain. His son momentarily dropped to his knees in front of him, hands hovering over the older man's injuries. “No, no, no, no- Why- Why did you-?”, Nox' voice broke, trying to fight the tears that were welling up in his eyes. He hastily got a hold of his father, as the elder threatened to topple over. “Why did you do that?!” They spent several seconds in that same position, a mixture between a hug and a desperate attempt at holding Zenathin steady. “I can't heal you, I barely know how to treat a simple wound. I'm so sorry. I-” When his father's cold fingers gently grazed the side of his face, Nox could not help but sob, salty tears mixing with the blood that now clung to his face too. The elder Shadar-Kai pulled down his son’s mask the last bit and pulled off his hood. Smiling at the sight, albeit faintly.

“I don't”, a flinch, “Regret – it.” His father took a shuddering breath, tears running down his face as well, “I – would do it again.” His smile wavered, “I regret- not being there- for you- and Solan. I- would go- I would go back if-”, his voice broke, small sobs replacing his words, as he fought the pain. Nox was crying too, his tears hitting his father's broken armour, “I'll- I'll get a healer- just-” Zenathin shook his head and his son cried harder. “I just got you back- I don't wanna loose you-”, there was no answer. “Father? No, no, please-”, he shook him once, twice, before his own body refused to comply. He did not move, even as steps grew closer.

backstory.title: Chapter X — A Mother's Love
paragraphs: The ground was swaying before his eyes. Or maybe he was swaying. He was not sure. His vision was blurred, unable to focus on anything, beyond the bright, painful light that filled the room. He could not move, any attempt of straightening his back, moving his arms or legs, ended in a pathetic whimper escaping his throat. But it was not from the pain, that he could not move an inch, not from the exhaustion at having not been allowed to rest for what felt like eternity. If his inner clock was anything to go by any more – he doubted it was – it had been at least two or three days. It had started what could have been a week ago. The torture. When the two members of the Radiant Church – one having the face of a woman once close to him, her voice, her words – entered the room, he had not expected what was awaiting him at that moment. After resisting the zone of truth once, the white robed man taught him to never dare such an act of defiance again. Shortly after he had regretted not defying them again, as a single word being spoken by the woman, who dared call herself his mother, pushed him to the brink of unconsciousness. Never again would he be able to hear the word 'pain' the same way again. Before this he had thought being punched and kicked by a bunch of grave-robbers, being shot or pushed into the canal of the waterfront district, almost being drowned by some vengeful people, was bad. But this was hell on earth. He had not talked but the session had ended with him curled up, pushed far back into the corner and not managing to bite down his tears.

The next day had not been any better. They had tried to convince him by offering him freedom, safety, comfort – anything if he admitted to killing their Templars. Every time he had declined, shut his mouth to not make a sound or stared them down with cold eyes, they had made him regret it. But again he did not talk. Even with them twisting his mind and memories, making him forget, making him believe, they did not manage to break him, no matter how hard they tried to alter his mind. Maybe his psyche would be easier, they surely had thought, as they changed their method for the next attempt once again. His hands pounded heavily against the ground, screaming out his lungs, or trying to, as the room he was in was suddenly engulfed in darkness, the light swallowed in a way that even his eyes could not pierce the shade, inky blackness closing in from all sides. When he had stopped hearing his own breathing afterwards, he had tried talking, then shouting. Now he was screaming, until there was no air left inside of him, before loosing his energy and dropping his balled fists that he could feel were bleeding from the rough stone. He remained frozen in place for what felt like hours. Finally, he pushed himself up, though it felt senseless, without actually being able to hear or see anything. He was desperately trying to find a way out. Maybe this was but a dream. He realised he was crying, when something wet dripped down onto his hands. And then, finally, he reached the wall. Or what had to be it, as his fingers felt nothing but sharp pain, when he grazed it’s surface. A warm, sticky substance ran down his wrists and arms little later, as he pulled back his injured hands, cradling them in front of him, feeling completely and utterly lost in a room covered in sharp spikes and without two of his senses to guide him. But even as the darkness faded and his ears could perceive again, as the walls returned to normal and the metal door was pushed open, revealing him cowering in the middle of the room, his spirit did not break. He did not talk.

The next time he fell asleep, not trance, as his frayed mind was no longer able to draw any form of rest from that, something was different. Something was off. Where his dreams usually showed a darkened outline of the Silverblood Castle’s hallways, he now found himself somewhere deep within the streets of the Spired District. Squinting up at the starless sky, he felt freezing winds stinging his face and hands. A shiver ran down his spine. He had not been aware one could feel cold – or anything for that matter, while dreaming. Looking around, his vision impaired by the sudden rise of a thick fog, worse than the unclear air of the Shrouded, he could barely make out a shape within the greyish blur. For a short moment he thought he was seeing the Shadow. But when his eyes managed to finally focus on the shape in front of him, his breath caught in his throat. Nox stumbled back, one step, two. Standing before him was Zenathin. Face bloodied from the graze of the other Templar’s sword, chest torn open from the arrow, that had torn him apart from the inside. Blood was dripping from the injury, steadily dropping down, down, down. The frosted white of the ground was slowly recoloured to a deep crimson red. As his father took a step forward, Nox drew a step back. Empty, lifeless eyes traced his movements sluggishly, no longer glowing white, as they had dulled to a feint grey. The assassin’s breath hitched, a choked sob escaping him, as the elder’s voice sounded. “This is all your fault. Tell them the truth.”

Nox woke with a start, tying uselessly to steady his breathing. To no avail. Tears were streaming down his face, he could not stop them. Even as exhaustion tugged at his senses, making him paranoid, tugging at his mind, forcing him into questioning reality, he forced himself to stay awake. When he could not take it any longer, he tranced, too afraid of dreaming again. Too afraid of having to face the image of his father once again. Even after the effects of the Dream spell wore off, Nox remained trapped in his own paranoia, in his own fear of sleep. But even the promise of making this stop, of letting him go, did not convince him to talk. Nothing did. And when they gave up on breaking his mind, they returned to breaking his body.

When they had returned the next day, at least he had guessed it would have been a day, they were holding a set of tools again. They forced him up and into a chair, tying something around his wrists and ankles that cut into his flesh instantly, drawing thick bands of blood from him. Later he would realise these things were a sort of barbed wire. He expected them to repeat the torture he had faced in the first days being here. But when the robed man heated a set of tweezers and a knife over a flame made by Eunoia, he realised it would be different from the last time. When she grasped his face and forced him to look up, something inside of him clicked and he came to the realisation that he would loose a part of himself if he kept quiet – literally. And then she forced his right eye open and his heart dropped. Never had he thought someone would – or could – hurt him this much physically. The glowing knife drawing ever closer to his eye, taking up his full vision, as tears started falling, burned into his memory. But his mouth remained closed when she asked him for the truth. The lie. He knew it would only get worse if he spoke. And so he kept quiet. Even when the knife took his vision, even when the tweezers were pushed into his skull and tore out what was left, piece by agonizing piece. The wet sound of blood soaked flesh falling to the floor almost broke him, almost forced him to talk. The tool was heated once again, before the man cut the final nerve, severing the eyestalk and finally drawing a sob from the Shadar Kai's lips. The cleric had smiled down at him. Or maybe he only imagined it. And then they had left him again. The day after, they did not go any easier on him. As they stood next to his chair on both sides, he already feared what was coming next. Despite desperately trying to hold his head up high, not let them see him beaten already, it was just too heavy to keep upright. If he had not been tied to the chair, he feared, he would have toppled over.

He had not seen it coming. His head was held underwater from one second to the next. Reflexively, he gasped for breath, only to feel salty water pour into his mouth, nose, down his throat, choking him, burning. His lungs were on fire. Everything was on fire. The right side of his face, surely crusted over with dry blood was practically set ablaze. And as his lungs filled with water, further and further, until all the usable oxygen in them flickered away and his body started convulsing to force him to breathe – finally draw in air – but in the process only worsened the situation, the world started spinning again. A sharp jab to his jaw brought him back to awareness, as he spat out more salty water than he remembered forcing itself down his throat. The warm, cosy blackness that had slowly started to engulf him, carrying him away from this horrible place to a better one was taken from him forcibly, replaced by the horrible reality of bright, stinging lights and icy cold water. But before his lungs could even fill themselves with sweet oxygen, burning from the abuse, his head was forced down again, back into the burning water.

And then they did not come back again. Leaving him to the bright light and the pain. He thought they were waiting for the blood loss to catch up with him, twisting his mind into a stupid act of weakness, to call out, to say what they wanted to hear from him. No matter if it was the truth. And now he wished he had died to his injuries. It would have prevented the torture of the next days. It would have prevented them from taking more. They were taking away everything he valued about himself. His ability to think clearly. His talent of seeing anything and everything, before it could draw too close. And now his ability to fight and kill. Because when they returned they might have started small at first. They started with needles, flattened little tools to heat up with magic until they were glowing red, before slowly pushing them into the flesh beneath his fingernails. The pain flared up instantly, drawing a scream from his already raw throat. At that moment in time he had not known it would get worse. But it did. Much worse. As they then continued with the tips of his fingers. They heated a way too dull knife and started with his index finger. It took him a moment to realise that the pathetic noise that filled the room, was his own plead for mercy. He did not want them to hear. But he could not keep in the sobs, or the whimpering as they took away each digit of his right hand. One by one. After several hours they left him. Now without his right hand, he watched them, silent tears and drops of blood mixing on the ground. Oh, how he wished to die.

But still they were not done with him. They returned to take more. He was not sure if this was still about the answers. They surely had enough witnesses. Loyal servants of the church that would say whatever was needed from them. They must have had 'proof' by now. But they wanted to hear him break. They wanted to hear him ruin himself. But even when they returned with the dull knife and turned to his arm, where they last left off, he did not break. They had already taken everything from him. There was nothing more they could threaten to take from him to cause him to slip up. This they would not take. They would not take his spirit. Staring down at his revealed bone, bile rose in his throat. Except that there was nothing he could actually force up. He had only gotten water. He stared down at his severed limb. The blood flow had partially been stopped by a piece of cloth firmly wrapped around his arm. Still, it did nothing to hide the two chalk white, but blood covered bones that protruded from the wound. This combined with the nauseating stench of burned flesh and the metallic taste of blood overwhelmed his senses and moments later, he spat out a mixture of blood and bile next to the chair he was on. And as the dark finally caught up to him, engulfing his senses in a warm, dark embrace, he only hoped that he may be allowed to rest even for only a few hours.

The next time the steel door was pushed open, only the woman entered. He looked up at her, his eyes – eye – barely able to focus with all the pain numbing his senses. She looked down at him, with her cold gaze, not even caring about the pain she caused her son, before she bent down. Only now did he see the bone-saw in her hand. She warned him, told him this was his last chance to be good. But he doubted he could speak up, even if he wanted to. He was not even able to scream, when she placed the saw against his upper arm and pushed. And pulled. And pushed again. The saw slowly tore through the flesh and muscle tissue, before reaching the bone. Every time he threatened to fall unconscious she held something up to his nose, waking him back into the living world. Barely living. And when the blood soaked piece of flesh hit the ground in a horribly loud splash, she regarded him, waiting for him to talk. And again, she was disappointed. He did not look at the piece of himself that had just been cut off without mercy. He also did not look up at the woman, who had once nursed him back to health and saved his life fifty-nine years ago, when he had been but a child. And he did not open his mouth. And he did not speak a single word. He kept staring ahead, promising himself that he would not give her the satisfaction of hearing a single word from him.

And then they did not return. They did not return for days. For weeks maybe. Nox could not tell. After countless hours of keeping his eyes trained upon the wall, he wondered if they would return again. Despite not knowing how long it had been, the tugging of hunger inside of him informed him that it had been days at the very least. His tongue was dry, the air stung, as he continued to suck in desperate gasps of breath. The shaking of his hands – hand made the barbed wire cut harder into his skin. Nox was freezing. He tried desperately to keep silent, to keep his teeth from clattering. The hunger stung. It was not the first time he was close to starving. But it was the first time he was incapable of doing anything to stop it. There was no getting away. There was no surviving this. This realisation struck hours, or maybe days later. He had completely lost all track of time. And of self. All his struggling resulted in nothing. Pleading with the empty air was equally useless. It seemed he was left entirely on his own. They left him. They left him to die. He was going to die of thirst, or starve, or bleed out. Whichever came first. Panic seized his senses, as the realisation struck. Desperate attempts at freeing his left arm drew whimpers from his lips that he hardly recognized as his own. He did not want to die. His mind was racing, rapid heartbeat drowning out his own cries soon after.

Freezing cold soon grasped at his heart. He did not know how long it had been. Nox had lasted weeks without anything to eat or clean water to drink. It could not have been that long, ever since they left him. Could it? The wire had loosened. Enough for him to free his hand. But it did not matter. He had fought to get up from the chair but instead of managing to stagger towards the door, he had toppled to the ground. The stone was freezing. Seeping all warmth left inside of him. He curled up, hand pressed against the wound on his arm. It had been cauterized, he noted distantly. Not that it mattered. Bleeding out slower did not change the fact he was bleeding out in the first place. It did not change the fact he was dying. Alone. Cold. Lying in a pool of his own blood.

Nox woke up. That simple fact alone was enough to startle him fully into awareness. The pain was back right with it, even though everything felt slowed, sluggish. His vision did not clear up for long moments. He was back in the chair, his tired brain noticed absently. The stabbing agony in his stomach returned, his throat burning with the stinging of thousands of tiny needles. Forcing his head up, Nox squinted at the silhouette of his mother. Diamond dust crumbled between her fingers. She had revived him, he realised with a start. Her cold eyes watched him closely, not speaking. She was waiting. Like a cat, ready to pounce on a downed bird. When she turned to leave, he almost reached out towards her frame. Nox felt like a child again, begging for his mother to hold him, to shield him from the pain, to safe him from death tugging at him, beckoning close. But Eunoia had never been the kind of woman to do such thing. To offer comfort. And just like back when he was a child, she was the one to reprimand him. She was the one, who caused him to suffer. A tiny sob came over his lips. He would never be able to describe the sensation of his heartbeat slowing down. Of his breath thinning out. Or his body growing colder. It would come to haunt him. Every time he felt the cold tugging at him. It would stand as a reminder whenever he closed his eyes. That haunting feeling. It burned into his memory. Burned hotter than the heated knives, cutting deep into his flesh. And when death returned to claim him, Nox was crying. Even if it was thirst that pried his life from his grasp, he somehow managed to cry.

Being dragged back into the land of the living was maybe worse than leaving in the first place. His breath caught in his throat, looking up at his mother again. Opening his mouth resulted in nothing but husky rasps grating her ears. As Eunoia grew annoyed with him, her hand reached for the side of his face. For a second that almost stretched into eternity, the touch felt comforting, left him helpless, begging for any semblance of proximity, no matter who offered it. But then her fingers dug into the scarring around his eye. When had it become scars? How long had he been here? “You can make it stop. You can make all of this stop.” She lingered, finger hovering over the now broken scarring. Blood dripped down his face, likely mirroring his tears. He forced his eye shut, shaking his head weakly. When he opened his eye again, the space in front of him was vacant. Eunoia had left him to die once again. He was going to die again. Over and over and over again. And maybe at some point his mother would decide not to bring him back. Nox could not tell what was worse. Tears continued to fall, mixing with the blood on the ground. He whispered into the empty air in front of him, begging for his mother to return. Begging for anyone to return. He did not want to die. Not again. His breath came in short, desperate huffs. Panic was squeezing his heart. Tears blurred his vision. But when the door cracked open, his eye still fixed on it. It must have been hours, at least. It was dark outside. Eunoia entered the room, forcing his head up to look at her. Her cold gaze dug into him, showing no trace of pity. No trace of love. To her, he had died long ago. “All you have to do is tell the truth.”

And he told her exactly what they wanted to hear. He told her and everyone who asked. It was not the truth, it was what they decided was the truth. From a thorn in the church's side as a former tool of the Silverbloods' he now became their scapegoat, a killer of their kin. The blood of three Templars, one of which his own father, was now on his hands. At least that was his truth from now on. He had expected them to kill him. But deep down he knew there was a reason they had wanted to break him. Why go through all the trouble just to end his life right after they were done? Granted, the Radiant Church did not always act in a way he could understand. Still, it would have been entirely nonsensical. Instead of killing him, they offered him his 'freedom', his life. They could use him. And his talents. For the death of Reinholdt Silverblood had changed the city. Even though the war had ended sometime during his absence, the city was facing a horrible future. There were beasts roaming the streets, looking to kill and feast on whatever or whomever they might find.

And Nox had killed two – three – of theirs. Not any plain members of the Church, but Grey Templars. He would pay for that. And he did. Still, they told him he could be of help. He could safe innocent lives rather than take them. They promised, he would only have to do what he did before. But not for the Silverbloods. He would be fighting for the Radiant Church. Or as they put it: The people of Luyarnha. He could do nothing but accept it when they put the Geas on him. The first one framing him as the murderer of the Templars, leaving no question. It forced him into silence about what went down behind the closed metal gates of the House of Blood. As if he was ever going to speak up about these past eight months. It was the only Geas spoken by his mother herself. The second one was put on him by a young woman serving under her. A devoted follower of the Radiant One. She grasped his shoulder, before telling him to never endanger or make a move against the Church, if it was not to protect the Radiant Order itself. And then there was the last Geas, put upon him that day, and every time he reported back to her. It was renewed, whenever he returned; Obey the Church’s order. No matter the cost.

Nox took aim at the creature down on the road of Paterna Iter, a white Militia-emblem hanging from his neck, dangling over the edge as he pulled the trigger of his rifle that was now entirely part of himself. That flowed into his right arm made up of an inky void, shadows connected to his flesh and his weapon. His grey hood, usually worn low enough to hide his features and be unaffected by winds, was knocked back, as he threatened to pull the trigger. Only his left eye locked upon the beast. When no shot rang and still the beast fell to the ground, the bullet dissolving into nothingness, as the shadows retreated, the task was done. The threat was handled and Luyarnha would have another safe harvest. Or so they all hoped. He had been sent into the district to 'clean it up'. Nox had understood then that he understood nothing. What he thought was a useless act of slaughtering beasts in the District that had moved to the rooftops a few months ago, had turned out to be a safekeeping mission for the food that said District now grew and harvested to feed the city. Without the full picture, he could not judge the Radiant Church. That did not mean they were right. But his hatred for them had clouded his vision and painted them as the lone villains. He agreed that, now that the Scourge had festered, his talents would have been wasted had he died that day by the hand of the Church. And he agreed that he was not fighting for the Silverbloods any more. Or for the Church. Or for himself. He was fighting for Luyarnha. Because he had fought for himself long enough. And for those who did not deserve fighters. And he had paid the price. He had left that part of himself behind, just like he had left Eunoia – a woman that still proclaimed herself his mother, after everything she had done. Now he was the city's weapon, only good for one thing: Killing the threats outside the walls. He wondered, if he was still alive. Or if he was nothing but a shell now. An eternal night that allowed for no more light. He wondered if it mattered. Maybe it would be enough to kill the Scourged, to keep the city safe, to fight in the imminent war, once it reached their walls.
To be the weapon Luyarnha needed. He hoped he would be enough.

backstory.title: Chapter XI — Of Choices and Chances
paragraphs: They had lied to him. Of course they had lied. Not even two weeks after becoming one of theirs – dropping the name 13 entirely, replaced by an equally soulless name, Hire – he was called in by one of the higher ranking members of the House of Blood. And this time, with the renewed Geas, he was given something else as well. A name. And the face of a man. A target. He had felt sick at the thought. They had claimed he would not have to kill another innocent again. He was certain the elf, the person he was meant to kill, was just that. Innocent. Hire had asked about the stranger’s crime. A mistake, he realised immediately, as the cleric’s eyes darkened.

Lysanthir Ileleste. Finding and following him was easy. And even though Nox- Hire’s entire skin crawled with the knowledge of what he was about to do, the Shadow trailed him effortlessly, silently waiting for the right moment to strike. He had thought he could leave all this behind. Never shoot someone in the back and then vanish, before anyone could take note of what happened. Never again. He had been wrong. Oh-so terribly wrong. He would never get away. He would never be able to change who or what he was. Deep down he would always be that unseen ghost, that indiscernible movement in the shadows. He would always be that assassin, that killer, that monster, with too much blood on his hands. Blood, that he would never be able to wash off. No matter how long he scrubbed at his hands under water, or how much he pried and scratched at the skin on his hands and arms. That blood would stay. And it would go on to stain everything he touched. He forced his eyes shut, trying to drown out the cascade of voices.

He could feel the Geas, like a wire wrapped around his throat, just like the barbed ones they had used to secure his arms to that wretched chair barely ten days ago. Ten days. He had yet to find Kadar. He could not imagine what seeing him again would be like, after all these months, months that should hardly matter in the face of his long, long life span. He could not shake the feeling of cold engulfing him, of loosing feeling in his entire body, slowly but surely. He could not shake the feeling of fear grasping at him, before that too vanished, leaving an empty void of nothing. No matter how desperately he tried shaking off the haunting memories, they remained, voices calling out to him, sensations washing over him, thoughts keeping his mind from wandering anywhere else.

Watching his target, trailing behind him, far enough to remain entirely hidden, he could not push away the voices, as he observed. Ileleste moved with determination, making his way through the District quickly, evidently hastening towards something, instead of away from it. He had a family. The voice in the back of Nox’ mind repeated over and over again. He had caught a glimpse of the elf’s wife and children. Something unfamiliar was seizing the assassin’s thoughts. Doubt, guilt, grief- Shaking off the sentiment, Nox pushed on, following his target out of the District and out of the city walls. This was it. This was his chance at striking him down without anyone around to witness. Of course, he could have shot him down from a few feet away, without any suspicions arising. No one would be able to pinpoint the origin of the killing shot. But then again, something had kept him from pulling the trigger. Maybe it was an irrational fear of someone figuring out that it had to have been a Shadow behind the murder. Or maybe it was, because he did not want to watch, as the elf’s body would be returned to his family. Maybe he dreaded seeing the pain in the children’s eyes. Because he knew he would not be able to walk away. He had never walked away. Not before seeing his target take their very last breath.

The path they were traversing lead to Jaegerweiler, Nox realised after another long moment. He briefly questioned why anyone would head there, after the acid flood. But just like the thought of why the Church wanted this innocent man dead, he pushed the question aside. It did not matter any longer.

It did not matter. Because the elf laid dying. The singular shot had pierced right through his heart. He would be bleeding out in a matter of seconds, minutes maybe. Nox waited, his breathing unsteady. He could not tell why he reacted like this. He had killed dozens, no, hundreds of people. He should not be this taken aback by a single name added to the list. He waited. Seeing the other’s writhing still, his breathing slowly thinning out, before coming to an even slower halt, Nox hesitantly separated from the shadows, walking closer. In the time in took to reach him, Lysathir Ileleste had taken his last breath. Nox pulled a white cloth from his pocket, carefully brushing it over the wound and collecting a trace of the still warm blood. He looked down at the corpse, laying so very still. Somehow the sight made him feel sick. Hesitantly, he bent down to close the man’s eyes, before turning and walking back towards the city.

backstory.title: Chapter XII — Fighting for What We Believe in
paragraphs: The beast fell, its head severed from the spine, pooling blackish, rancid blood onto the dirt ground and mixing it into a blubbering, stinking mess that emitted a foul smell, almost causing the hunters to double over. Sirenn, ever the leader, used his curved dagger to cut off its ears and pocketed them, not minding the ruination it caused his clothing. Nox sent Malik back into the air to keep a lookout, as they returned to the city, its high walls blocking the sun from their view.

“So, first hunt, correct?”, Sirenn wiped the dagger on his pants before sheathing it and letting it slip back into his pocket. The Tiefling next to him slowly nodded, eyes locked on the dripping ears. “My family said it was the only way I could be useful to the city. So I joined the Radiant Church. They seemed keen to have me join them.” “They always do”, said Sirenn. His fondness of the Church could be measured on the very tip of his dagger, after having been told about his payment being a home in the Cathedral for his family. Apparently he had told them to fuck themselves and give him proper payment. Later he had mentioned his parents being killed by the Silverbloods for being believers. Nox understood his anger at the Church's way well. It had taken a while for them to agree paying a fair price for the hunts.

“It is a great honour being able to hunt with a Jaegar by my side on my first trip out”, Hessia explained, eagerly jogging up next to the Scourgeborne, after having fallen back a slight bit. Nox remembered having said the same thing. Sirenn had laughed at this heartedly, firmly grabbed his shoulder and pulled him closer to tell him that it would not be the last time. This time, the hunter patted her shoulder, “You newbies always say such bull. You'll see it's horrible working with me. But jokes on you. You're stuck with me, cuz you're one of the good ones!”, he grinned, almost indistinguishably as his teeth were always visible anyway.  “One of the good ones?”, she smiled, looking at his clawed hand. “You're not doing this for money. Or fame. You want to make your family proud. That is what he means to say.” Nox said from the shadows of the trees, as they made their way closer to the graveyard. Hessia seemed surprised, “I thought you couldn't speak.”

Nox laughed silently, drowned out by Sirenn's amused snort, “That's cuz he barely does.” A little later Hessia spoke up, voice thin, as to not disturb the dead around them. “But do tell. How do you know I am not doing this for myself?” “Well”, Sirenn patted the side of his pants, “If you did this only for money, you would want to carry the ears. If you did this for fame, you would have wanted to take the head instead. Or get the final blow. But instead, you protected Nox over 'ere, when the beast spotted him. You did not use the chance to kill it and risk you comrade's life, nah, you lured it back for us to finish it. Smart, brave and selfless. I like ya.” Nox nodded faintly at the explanation, still keeping an ear out for the dangers that lurked in the darkness.

When they returned to the city, they followed the lively street in the Paterna Iter District back towards the Grand Cathedral and after accepting their payment, the hunters were back on their way. Only, when Sirenn and Nox were about to leave the inner circle, they were approached by a member of the Militia, wearing its emblem proudly on his chest. “Hunters, halt over there! You two seem like two capable fighters of great calibre. We are in need of some well-trained fighters for tonight's match in the Garden of Eden.
